'''Dorothy Jean Phillips''' (née Wingfield) (born July 27, 1945) is an American [[chemist]] and 2025 President of the [[American Chemical Society]]. She worked on circular dichroism and bioseparation. In 1967, Phillips was the first African-American woman to complete a bachelor's degree at [[Vanderbilt University]]. She later earned her doctorate in biochemistry in 1979 from the University of Cincinnati.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Dorothy J. Wingfield Phillips |url=https://www.vanderbilt.edu/trailblazers/person/dorothy-phillips/ |access-date=2026-11-03 |website=Vanderbilt University |language=en-US}}</ref> 

== Early life and education ==
Phillips grew up in segregation in the southern United States.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2013/december/dorothy-j-phillips-elected-to-board-of-worlds-largest-scientific-society.html|title=Dorothy J. Phillips elected to board of world's largest scientific society|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> She was one of eight children. Her father, Reverend Robert Cam Wingfield, worked as a porter for the Greyhound Bus station before attending classes at the American Baptist Theological Seminary to become a [[Baptists|Baptist]] minister.<ref name=":1" /> Her mother, Rebecca Cooper Wingfield, did occasional domestic work.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xBhnDwAAQBAJ&q=dorothy+J.+Phillips&pg=PA5|title=African American Women Chemists in the Modern Era|last=Brown|first=Jeannette E.|date=2018-08-08|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780190615185|language=en}}</ref> As a young girl the only white people Phillips knew were those who had employed her mother.<ref name=":1" />

Her parents were very supportive of her education, and attended local meetings of the ''Negro'' [[Parent–teacher association|Parent Teachers Association]].<ref name=":1" /> The Wingfields became more active with the [[civil rights movement]] after the [[Rosa Parks]] bus boycott in 1956.<ref name=":1" /> Her brother was part of the [[Nashville sit-ins]] and her family were one of the first to integrate into [[Nashville, Tennessee|Nashville]]. Phillips attended a [[National Science Foundation]] summer school for African-American students, which inspired her to study chemistry.<ref name=":1" /> She and her boyfriend took part in a statewide mathematics competition 'for colored students'.<ref name=":1" /> She eventually majored in [[chemistry]] at [[Tennessee State University]], but transferred to [[Vanderbilt University]] in 1966.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vanderbilt.edu/celebratingblackhistory/whowaswho/index.php|title=Who Was Who|website=Celebrating Black History|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>

While Phillips originally intended to study medicine, she was discouraged by her advisor who believed she would not be able to have a family and attend [[medical school]].<ref name=":1" /> She pledged to the [[Alpha Kappa Alpha]] sorority.<ref name=":1" /> She studied chemistry at [[Vanderbilt University]], where she was the first African-American woman to earn a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in 1967.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|url=https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2017/07/18/dorothy-phillips-first-african-american-woman-to-receive-an-undergraduate-degree-from-vanderbilt-recognized/|title=Dorothy Phillips, first African American woman to receive an undergraduate degree from Vanderbilt, recognized|last=Communications|first=Vanderbilt Division of|website=Vanderbilt University|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> Attending [[Vanderbilt University]] was the first time Phillips had white classmates and professors.<ref name=":1" /> After graduating, Phillips worked in [[psycho-pharmaceutical]] research.<ref name=":1" /> She completed her doctoral studies at the [[University of Cincinnati]], and, again, was the first African-American woman in [[Cincinnati]] to earn a PhD in [[biochemistry]].<ref name=":1" />

In 1973 the joined the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.aaas.org/events/facebook-live-opportunities-serve-human-rights|title=Facebook Live: Opportunities to Serve Human Rights|website=American Association for the Advancement of Science|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> She worked on the R17 virus, using [[circular dichroism]] and [[electron paramagnetic resonance]] to understand the conformation of the viral protein.<ref name=":1" /> Whilst researching the R17 virus, Phillips read about the work of Patrick Oriel at [[Dow Chemical Company]], and decided to apply.<ref name=":1" />

== Career ==
After graduating, Phillips joined the [[Dow Chemical Company]] as a bench scientist.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.soflacs.org/nlettapr17.pdf|title=American Chemical Society South Florida Section Newsletter|website=ACS South Florida Section|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref><ref name="Philips, Dorothy">{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/acs-webinars/presenters/philips-dorothy.html|title=Philips, Dorothy|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28|archive-date=2019-03-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190328225428/https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/acs-webinars/presenters/philips-dorothy.html|url-status=dead}}</ref> She developed [[circular dichroism]] and began to work on antibiotics and herbicides.<ref name=":1" /> At [[Dow Chemical Company]] Phillips helped students from [[Michigan State University]] to analyse the antibiotics in animal feed. She established how they might impact animal growth.<ref name=":1" /> She is responsible for several patents in the area, including one to improve lactation and another to improve feed utilisation.<ref>{{Citation|title=Method for improving lactation in ruminant animals|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4534969A/en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=(Trichloromethyl)pyridine compounds useful for promoting growth and/or improving feed utilization efficiency in ruminants|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4474789A/en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref><ref>{{Citation|title=3-Trichloromethyl-5-substituted-1,2,4-thiadiazoles as ruminant animal growth promoters|url=https://patents.google.com/patent/US4543357A/en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>

Phillips joined the [[Waters Corporation]] in 1984, where she worked in research and development until 1996.<ref name=":3">{{Cite web|url=http://analyzersource.blogspot.com/2017/|title=The Analyzer Source|website=analyzersource.blogspot.com|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> At [[Waters Corporation]] Phillips was a member of the Chemical Research and Development department, developing [[chromatography]] packing materials and bioseparations.<ref name=":1" /> Under her leadership the team developed the ''AccellPlus'' exchange packings, which could be used to separate proteins.<ref name=":1" /> She began to consult the biotechnology company [[Millipore Corp.]], travelling the world to talk about the work of the [[Waters Corporation]].<ref name=":1" /> Her work expanded to include [[high-performance liquid chromatography]]. Phillips also investigated small molecules, including the drug [[sildenafil]].<ref name=":1"/> She served as Clinical Marketing Director and Strategic Marketing Director.<ref>{{Cite journal|date=2016-09-12|title=Dorothy J. Phillips|journal=C&EN Global Enterprise|language=en|volume=94|issue=36|pages=56–58|doi=10.1021/cen-09436-acsnews010|issn=2474-7408|doi-access=free}}</ref> She was involved with the development of the [[Waters Corporation]] Symmetry columns and Oasis cartridges.<ref name=":3" /> At both the Dow Chemical Company and Waters Corporation, Phillips moved from research development to business management.<ref name=":5">{{Cite web|title=Statement with Video|url=http://www.dorothyphillips.net/statement-with-video.html|access-date=2021-03-28|website=Dorothy J. Phillips, Ph.D.|language=en}}</ref> After an almost thirty-year career, Phillips retired from the [[Waters Corporation]] in 2013 s Director of Strategic Marketing .<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|last=Robertson|first=Seth|title=Trailblazing alumna Dorothy Phillips discusses her career as a chemist, importance of diversity in the physical sciences|url=https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2020/10/02/trailblazing-alumna-dorothy-phillips-discusses-her-career-as-a-chemist-importance-of-diversity-in-the-physical-sciences/|access-date=2021-03-28|website=Vanderbilt University|language=en}}</ref> Phillips has been elected the American Chemical Society president in 2025 and immediate past president in 2026. <ref>{{Cite web |last=Cottle |first=Sara |date=2025-01-21 |title=Dorothy J. Phillips elected 2024 American Chemical Society president-elect |url=https://cen.acs.org/acs-news/elections/Dorothy-J-Phillips-elected-2024-American-Chemical-Society-president-elect/101/i37 |access-date=2026-01-15 |website=Chemical & Engineering News |language=en}}</ref> A total of 11,428 votes were cast for president-elect. With 6,653 votes, Phillips won the president-elect race against Florian J. Schattenmann, chief technology officer and vice president of research and development and innovation at [[Cargill]], who received 4,775 votes. Phillips became the first Black woman to serve as president of the American Chemical Society in 2025.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Chalk |first=Dan |date=2025-02-10 |title=Former Midlander is first Black woman to lead American Chemical Society |url=https://www.ourmidland.com/news/article/former-midlander-first-black-woman-lead-american-20158310.php |access-date=2026-02-06 |website=Midland Daily News |language=en}}</ref> 

=== Academic service ===
In 1990 Phillips became involved with the [[American Chemical Society]] Northeastern Section.<ref name="Philips, Dorothy"/> She was involved with the [[American Chemical Society]] Project SEED, an initiative which allows high school students from disadvantaged backgrounds to complete summer placements in research laboratories.<ref name=":1" /> As a candidate in 2013 for the position of director-at-Large for the American Chemical Society, Phillips stated that if she were elected to the position, she would aim to address two issues: global chemistry enterprise and chemical safety.<ref name=":5" /> In 2013 Phillips was appointed director-at-large of the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref name=":0" />  Since 2014, Phillips has served as the [[American Chemical Society]] board liaison for the society's Science and Human Rights program. This program monitors the cases of scientists worldwide whose rights have been abridged.  She was re-elected as director-at-Large in 2016, and seeks to use her tenure to improve their 'globalization and diversity'.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2016/november/dorothy-phillips-of-natick-reelected-to-acs-board.html|title=Dorothy J. Phillips of Natick, Massachusetts re-elected to board of world's largest scientific society|website=American Chemical Society|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> In 2017 [[Vanderbilt University]] created two faculty fellowships in her honour.<ref name=":2" /> The inaugural fellowship holder was [[Renã A. S. Robinson]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.vumc.org/vmac/person/rena-s-robinson-phd|title=Renã A. S. Robinson, PhD {{!}} Vanderbilt Memory & Alzheimer's Center|website=www.vumc.org|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> In the fall of 2019, Philips was re-elected to serve a third term in 2020 on the board of directors for the [[American Chemical Society]].<ref>{{Cite web|title=American Chemical Society announces election results for 2020 officers|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2019/november/acs-announces-election-results-for-2020-officers.html|access-date=2021-03-28|website=American Chemical Society|language=en}}</ref>

Phillips' awards and honours include;

* 1994 [[University of Cincinnati]] Distinguished Alumni<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.artsci.uc.edu/content/dam/artsci/departments/chemistry/Docs/ChemBond2010.pdf|title=CHEMBOND|website=University of Cincinnati|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>
* 2004 [[American Chemical Society]] Nashville Section Salute to Excellence Award<ref name=":4">{{Cite web|url=http://www.dorothyphillips.net/honors.html|title=Honors|website=Dorothy J. Phillips, Ph.D.|language=en|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>
* 2006 [[Vanderbilt University]] Unsung Heroine Award<ref name=":4" />
* 2006 [[American Chemical Society]] Northeastern Section Henry A. Hill Award<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.nesacs.org/awards/hill/awards_hill_recipients.html|title=Welcome to NESACS - Awards {{!}} Henry A. Hill Award Recipients|website=www.nesacs.org|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>
* 2008 [[American Chemical Society]] Santa Clara Valley Section Shirley B. Radding Award<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://svacs.org/?page_id=44|title=Awards and Grants {{!}} American Chemical Society|language=en-US|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.svacs.org/newsletter/news0808.pdf|title=Silicon Valley Chemist|website=SVACS|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>
* 2008 [[Waters Corporation]] Leadership Award for Outstanding Contributions<ref name=":1" />
* 2008 [[Vanderbilt University]] Dr. Dorothy Wingfield Phillips Award for Leadership
* 2010 Fellow of the [[American Chemical Society]]<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/88/i31/2010-ACS-Fellows.html|title=2010 ACS Fellows {{!}} August 2, 2010 Issue - Vol. 88 Issue 31 {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>
* 2011 [[New England]] Institute of Chemists Distinguished Chemist Award<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://cen.acs.org/content/cen/articles/94/i36/DirectorLarge-Dorothy-J-Phillips.html|title=For Director-at-Large: Dorothy J. Phillips {{!}} Chemical & Engineering News|website=cen.acs.org|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref>
* 2015 [[Vanderbilt University]] Dr. Dorothy J. Wingfield Phillips Endowed Chair
*2019 [[Vanderbilt University]] Member of the inaugural class of Vanderbilt Trailblazers <ref>{{Cite web|last=Blue|first=Jalen|title=Five Vanderbilt Trailblazer portraits unveiled during Reunion Weekend|url=https://news.vanderbilt.edu/2019/10/19/five-vanderbilt-trailblazer-portraits-unveiled-during-reunion-weekend/|access-date=2021-03-28|website=Vanderbilt University|language=en}}</ref>
*2020 [[National Organization for the Professional Advancement of Black Chemists and Chemical Engineers]]  Lifetime Achievement Award.<ref>{{Cite web|title=2020 NOBCChE Lifetime Achievement Award Presented to Dorothy J. Wingfield-Phillips, Ph.D.|url=https://acswcc.org/2020-nobcche-lifetime-achievement-award-presented-to-dorothy-j-wingfield-phillips-ph-d/|access-date=2021-03-28|website=acswcc.org|date=30 September 2020 |language=en-US}}</ref>

=== Personal life ===
Phillips was married two weeks after graduating from [[Vanderbilt University]]. Her brother, Robert C. Wingfield, serves as director of the Fisk Community Environmental Toxics Awareness and Sustainability Program.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.fisk.edu/directory/robert-wingfield/|title=Robert Wingfield {{!}} Fisk University|website=www.fisk.edu|access-date=2019-03-28}}</ref> She has two children, Anthony and Crystal, and a step-daughter called Vickie.<ref name=":1" />
